definite refusal answers 412 with the remedy at once

(another fm binary or OS build, another server identity
or digest) is answered 412, no probe

starts no probe of that key for one Retry-After interval

An unknown key (design-managed-servers-2026-11-09.md, section 17 item
10, which replaces section 6.3). A key with a component that cannot be
read is UnknownKey. The one rule: a probe result is read from or
written to the record store only under a key whose every component was
read. Under UnknownKey a request reads no record; the gateway measures
the running server instance by the same automatic probe (503 with
Retry-After while it runs), keeps the result in memory for that
instance only (mem), and measures again when the instance starts again
(InstanceRestart, and the gateway's own Crash and Restart). The flight
under UnknownKey is the gateway's in-memory flight: no lock file names
an unknown key, and the CLI keeps nothing from such a measurement. A
probe that spans a key change or an instance start keeps nothing.
Why AutoProbe.endpoint sets Unreadable FALSE (section 17 item 14). The
key of this model (Keys, worldKey) is what a current record must match.
For a managed server it is the record key itself, the binary's sha256
and the OS build; both are read from the host, and either read can fail
(Unreadable). For an endpoint, the record key of section 6.1 is the
settings' endpoint and model
(packages/config/src/probe-record-key.ts (EndpointProbeKey, endpointKeyOf)).
Nothing in it is read from the host, so it is never unknown,
and the unknown-key path of item 10 cannot arise for an endpoint
target. The model's key of an endpoint stands for the identity the
server reports, which a record must match
(packages/gateway/src/probe/record.ts (recordForIdentity); "The key
source" below). A failed
read of that identity, like any failed request to the endpoint, is the
existing transient error described below, not an unknown key.
Flights per key, instances elsewhere (section 17 items 3 and 12). The
probes of this model are flights per record key, with the record lock
of each key (SingleProbePerKey). A probe instance is an owner and a
target, and a flight under a newer key waits for the running flight of
its instance before it starts its server; that wait is ManagedServer.tla
(InstanceWait, OneLiveChild). Here it only delays the flight's end,
which EndProbe, at any time, already covers.
Failure kinds. A definite refusal of a precondition (the licence is not
agreed, the model is not available, the binary is missing) is the world
state refused, which the user toggles (Refuse, Fix); it is not
remembered. A probe that started and failed is Fail; a gateway probe
that fails puts its key in backoff until BackoffEnds (one interval). A
stop of the gateway (Crash) ends its probes without a failure: no
backoff, and the in-memory backoff is gone after Restart.
The key source. The fm key is the binary sha256 and the OS build. The
gateway caches it by the binary's file identity (device, inode, size,
modification time), so a replaced binary is seen by the next request.
The OS build is read with the cache and can change only by an OS
update, which restarts the machine and so the gateway: OsUpdate is
enabled only while the gateway is down. An endpoint key changes when
the server reports another identity (chat-completions: the identity of
the listed model; ollama: the model digest), at any time (BinaryChange
stands for an identity change of every adapter). A record of another
key is no record: the request takes the probe path, never a 412 for the
mismatch (packages/gateway/src/probe/record.ts (recordForIdentity)).
An identity read that failed (a labelled outbound error) is not an
action of the model. The request fails with that transient error; the
code sets the current identity to unknown before each read, so the
failure writes no record, starts no probe and leaves no key behind
(packages/gateway/test/identity-read-failure.test.ts (createProbedEndpointTarget, createProbedOllamaTarget)).
The step changes
only an answer that is neither 200 nor 412, which RecordMatchesKey does
not constrain. A key kept from an earlier read is KeyView "atStart",
whose evidence AutoProbe.keyAtStart already violates RecordMatchesKey.

P2: no response is built from a guessed capability
P3: a request with no record gets 503, never 412 or 200, and the 503

P8: a definite refusal of a precondition answers 412 with the remedy at

P9: no gateway probe of a key starts inside its backoff interval
P10: every record is written by a probe that held the lock of its key
P4: after the record is written, or the result kept in memory under an

P5: a failed probe never writes a record

P11: no record is written under an unknown key (section 17 item 10)

holds what adoption needs: the unsent input, the viewport anchor with
its following flag, the display toggles (thought entries folded or
open), the number of printed items (scrollback), the negotiation state.
When the value is lost (envKnown false) the new process leaves every
mode of the table once (LeaveAll), then starts as an ordinary client in
the screen mode of its settings (screenNow), and adopts the record.
The model's four modes stand for the two kinds of rows of the mode
table: alt and mouse and paste are idempotent rows (a second enter
write changes nothing in the terminal; paste stands for focus and
modify-other-keys too); kitty is a stacked row (a second push needs a
second pop; it stands for the title stack too). Every action treats
every row alike, so the number of rows does not change a result.
Abstracted away, with the reason:
- the clock and every duration: no rule of the design reads one;
- the contents of the record beyond the copied fields, the daemon, the
replay and the store: the screen is one fold of the events (16.1);
- the row offset of the anchor and the terminal size: the adoption runs
the live resize path (screens 2.5), which clamps the offset and keeps
following; only the entry key and following are checked (ViewKept),
and no modelled variable reads the size;
- the order of escape sequences inside one write, the terminal replies
(a mode appears when its reply arrives: EnableMouse), the negotiation
state is one bit fixed before the first move;
- the effect of a /tui switch on the screen mode: Screen is fixed per
behaviour; a switch under way is not a quiet point (switching blocks
Begin), so no move sees a switch half done and no switch changes the
mode set of a move;
- the leave at session exit: it writes the leave sequence of the same
enabled set by the same table as LeaveAll and Refuse, no second actor;
- /clear (it opens a new session, so no record holds a clear mark); the
ACP, attach and headless kinds (they have no screen).
The terminal state changes only by writes of the product.

An instance is an owner, a target and a purpose, with its own socket
and marker directory (managed items 4, 8, 12, 13; 18.2.1). The owner is
a generation's gateway (scope g) or the CLI, which lies outside every
generation (scope 0, managed item 13, 18.2.7). Per scope and target
there are three instances and four flights:
instance "s"  the serving instance, owned by the gateway; its one
flight is also called "s"
instance "g"  the gateway's probe instance; flights "p1" and "p3".
"p3" is a second gateway flight of the target under a
newer key, started while "p1" still runs under the
older key (a key change taints the running flight)
instance "c"  the CLI's probe instance (item 13), in another process;
its flight "p2"
The children on an instance are the live children of its flights
(alive) and the children an earlier owner left in its socket and
marker directory (orphan). The state of an instance is kept under its
key, KeyS(scope): the image of the instance path of 18.2.1. With the
product's key, KeyS is the scope itself; the evidence SharedKey maps
every generation to one key, as the path without a generation would.
Generations (I5, 18.2.2). A generation g has a gateway gw[g]: none,
up or down. It retires (ret[g]) when a newer generation has started
(the role poll of 18.1; Retire). A retiring gateway accepts no new
call and starts no flight (rule 3, 4.2.3, 18.1): StartServe and a
gateway ProbeStart need ~ret. The accepted calls of a generation are
calls[g][t], at most MaxCalls; a call is accepted only while serving
(Accept), and it ends by its own bound (CallEnd). A restart of a child
by its timer (TimerFires) needs a serving gateway or an accepted call
that needs the child (18.1.5, GwNoRestartRetiring). Two generations of
one target run in parallel: a flight of generation g waits only for the
running flight of its own instance (InstanceWait), never for another
generation's (rule 4, 18.2.2). The probe record lock is outside this
model (18.3), so the per-key switch SingleFlight relates only flights
that share a lock (Locked, below).
Item 12: one flight of an instance runs at a time. A flight under a
newer key takes its record key's lock (the per-key kernel lock stays
for the record, P10 and P11 in AutoProbe.tla), then waits ("wait") for
the running flight of its instance, and enters when that flight has
ended. The wait has no clock of its own: it ends when the running
flight ends, and every state of that flight ends at its own bound
(WaitsEnd). The claim of the socket is not that exclusion: the evidence
sharedProbeSocket (InstanceWait FALSE) has two flights of one target
under different keys both pass their claims on the instance's one

(packages/gateway/src/managed/server.ts (claimInstance, waitForFreeSocket):
the reap, then the socket check), and both spawn: OneLiveChild is violated.
The instance name recurs across starts, because the start-time reap of
the same instance is what removes an orphan (StartAfterOrphanServes is
per instance); a name per flight, such as a key digest, never recurs
once the key changes.
Item 13: the CLI's instance has its own socket and marker directory
outside every generation, so no generation reaper and no supervisor

Item 15 and decision 12: a survivor is retried a bounded number of
times, then the person is told. The first attempt to stop a child is
its own stop (StopEnd; for a gateway that crashed, the supervisor's
reap). A child that survives it is a survivor, and every later reap of

Abstractions. Time is nondeterministic: each wait ends by its own
completion or by its asking limit (A1). The child's readiness, crash
and exit are environment events (A2). A live child holds its socket, so
the claim's socket check sees every live child on its key. A measurement
ends in a report, a failure or its limit, which have the same effect
here (A6). Generations are scopes (A4): a generation's gateway, its
instances and its calls; the content of a call is not modelled, and a
call is one counter. Marker file contents and the reaper's signalling
are ProcessMarker.tla and ProcessStop.tla (A5). The retries of an
instance are one count (tries) for its survivors: in the holding
configurations an instance has at most one child on it (OneLiveChild),
so the count is that survivor's attempt record. Which of decision 12's
four occasions a retry is (before the next process or file call, the
periodic check, start-up, shutdown) is not modelled; every retry of the
model spends one, so the model admits more retries at one occasion than
the product makes, never more retries in all.
Fairness and the environment. The asking limits, the stops, the
restart timer, the instance's entry after its wait, the end of the
claim, the supervisor's reap, the end of a call and the role poll are
weakly fair; nothing is strongly fair. The environment's events are
bounded, each by its own counter: gateway closes (MaxCloses), gateway
crashes, CLI cancels and kills, key changes, child crashes and refusal
toggles. A close or a crash may cut a claim (the model's Close moves it
to stopping; in the code the claim runs to its own outcome first
(packages/gateway/src/managed/server.ts (performStart, runRestart)),
and the stop waits for the pending start
(packages/gateway/src/managed/server.ts (stop, startFlight))); with the
closes bounded, a claim that recurs ends by
its own outcome, and weak fairness does not choose that outcome: the
kept reap stays possible each time. A behaviour with more closes than
MaxCloses is not checked.

The rule (AttemptOnReject = TRUE)
- the key of a call is (run, step, attempt)
- a claim that resends a recorded request keeps the attempt, so the
gateway replays the stored answer or joins the call in flight
- when the runtime rejects a complete answer it records the rejection
with that attempt before the claim ends; the next claim resends the

frames and streaming are not modelled; a charge is one count per
recorded outcome (charged). In the code a rejection's charge is a
usage.charged event (purpose rejected_answer) appended atomically
with model.rejected, and an acceptance's charge is model.responded
- the meter's counter is read once at claim start (mCtr) from the
gateway's counter; the gateway's counter changes a bounded number
of times at any moment (a gateway restart with a new target
definition). An in-flight call keeps the counter it started with
- the upstream call is one action (start) and one action (finish);
the gateway survives a crash of the runtime, and a call in flight
finishes and is stored
- the gateway's store is never lost and never expires
- every claim that ends without an accepted answer (crash or
rejection) uses one of MaxClaims attempts of the run; when they are
used up the run is FAILED
- the other failure and retry paths of the step (compaction
recovery, deadline, cancel, stream restart) are not modelled
- the recording of the rejection and of the accepted answer is one
atomic append each
- the outcome (accept or reject) is charged once, when it is recorded:
the event model.rejected carries the usage of the rejected answer and
the run's spend counts it (charged); a replayed answer costs nothing

against its own counter from the claim's listing

header: Design model of the credential lifecycle of a ChatGPT plan account in
the gateway (design-chatgpt-plan.md sections 5 and 9, increments P5a
and P5b). It describes what the design says the code does.
Modelled
- the account record on disk (an atomic register): state, generation,
refresh token, cause, pendingRefresh, issue time, subject
- the memory copy: state, generation, refresh token, dirty flag,
issue time, the generation of the last forced refresh
- the server's token family: single-use rotating refresh tokens, a
consumed token presented again revokes the family, a revoked family
answers every refresh with a terminal code, the user's disconnect
- the per-account FIFO mutex, held across the token-endpoint call
- requests: read (single flight), 401 recovery with coalescing
- the refresh POST as a packet in flight: it can be answered, given
up by the client (timeout, lost response) and still reach the
server later, or be orphaned by a crash and still reach the server
- sign-in install, sign-out with revocation, persist retry, crash
and restart (volatile state lost, a record in signing_out resumes)
Abstractions (a proof holds only for this model)
- token values are small integers; a token belongs to the family
issued at or after sStart
- time is a discrete clock; an access token is Fresh at age 0, Near
(inside the margin M, refresh first) at age 1 and Stale (inside the
skew S, never sent) from age 2; clock skew, the values of L, S, B
and M, and earliest_refresh_at are the Z3 proof plan-refresh
- a refresh attempt ends answered, or given up (a timeout or lost
response: nothing is known about the server). After a give-up the
client may resend the same token up to MaxResend times in the same
request while holding the mutex (ReqRetry), or end the refresh as a
transient failure at any give-up; the count is per request. The
backoff and the Retry-After cap are the Z3 proof plan-refresh
- the ID token, the JWKS, the scope verdict and PKCE are a candidate
subject and the client id of the registration the authorization
came from (inSrc); PlanSignIn models the attempt
- the exchange of a code and the install are one step; a crash
before the install leaves the record unchanged, the same as not
starting
- invalid_client and the state plan_disabled are not modelled: they
keep every token, so they cannot affect the properties
- the file system is an atomic register; a crash during a write
leaves the old or the new record, which are the states before and
after the write step
- the redactor, HTTP bodies, the 401 status of the Responses call:
the server answers a request with success, or with 401 when the
family is revoked or the 401 budget allows (a skewed or rejected
access token)
- the answer of the server to a revocation of a consumed token is the
pessimistic reading of open item O4: an empty 200 that revokes only
the token it names, so the family stays live when the token named
is not the current one
- the 30-day refresh token expiry is a Disc (disconnect) step
- a persist failure is transient (retried, MaxPersistFail) or
deterministic (MaxDetFail): the memory state store_unwritable, mUnwr
is memory only, requests go on while the token is not Stale, no
refresh starts, no retry, and a later write fails for the same
cause; sign-in and sign-out writes in that state fail without
effect. A failure of the intent write before a refresh is not a
step of the model: the code
(packages/gateway/src/plan/session.ts (refreshUnderLock, writeRecord))
records the write failure, sends nothing and ends that refresh, so
nothing is consumed
- a restart may find the record unreadable (MaxUnreadable): the
memory state store_unreadable with no tokens, the disk untouched;
sign-in and sign-out do not start; a later restart reads again
- a 200 from the token endpoint with an unusual body (MaxNoAdopt, up to
that many): WeakForms picks what it was. short: the server rotated and
sent a replacement with expires_in <= M. noRtRotated: the server
consumed the token and sent no replacement. noRtKept: the server sent
no replacement and did not consume the token (RFC 6749 section 6, an
issuer that does not rotate). NoAdoptRule is what the client does.
adopt (the rule taken, design 14.4 item 5): every 200 is adopted; a
replacement is stored in the same write, else the access token is
taken and the old refresh token is kept. The other rules exist only as
evidence of rules not taken. transient: keep everything, resend
allowed (design section 7 as it was). reject: keep everything, end
the refresh, no resend inside it. unanswered: count it as an
unanswered send (a slack credit), resend allowed. signIn: clear the
tokens with the evidence cause transient. A rotated successor that the
client never holds is dropped[a]
- why noRtRotated cannot be kept whole by any rule: the server consumed
the token and never sent its successor, which violates RFC 6749
section 6 and F7 (a replacement on every refresh). The client holds
only the consumed token and cannot tell this from noRtKept. Any rule
that sends the stored token later gets a terminal code (SingleUse
Server refuted, PlanCredential.weakAdoptRotated); a rule that never
sends it ends a healthy session in noRtKept (NoEraseOnTransient
refuted, PlanCredential.weakSignInKept). What is checked instead:
SingleUseUnlessSilent (the part of I-C3 not excused by a server that
consumed a token silently, silentRot) and that the loss is detected
(LossDetected, I-C7), keeps the registration and records the server
code and the interrupted flag as they were
- interrupted: the record flag dInt that an earlier send of the same
token went unanswered. rint[r] is the knowledge of the request: set
from the pendingRefresh found when this refresh began (left by an
earlier attempt or loaded at restart, not the one this refresh writes
next) and by a give-up earlier in this refresh. dCause is always the
server code (LegacyCause = TRUE restores the old behaviour:
refresh_interrupted whenever dPend is set)

something loads the account (a request, a listing, the start of a
sign-in); no timer does it. SoReload is weakly fair in the model, so
SigningOutResolves holds in the code only if such a load happens

- after SoAbort the code drops its memory copy and reads the record

header: The run lock of development tooling (design-dev-run-reuse, section 3): a heavy run never overlaps any other
run, light runs may overlap each other. Protocol: claim your own lock first, then look at the other class.

(HClaimHeavy, HScanOne, HDecide) including its removal of a free light file left by a dead holder, the release
by the holder (LEnd, HEnd), a crash of any process at any step with the kernel freeing its lock (Crash), a
waiter that repeats attempts up to its own limit (Retry, GiveUp), a nested child that inherits the token of a
running holder (KSpawn, KEnd, KCrash). Two starts at the same instant are two processes whose steps interleave.
A describer and an isHeld probe only read and are invisible to the protocol (a probe is retried by the claim).

the heavy has claimed (todo is a snapshot); a light that claims later is refused by its own look at heavy.
